# **Overview** {#overview}

This unit explores how artificial intelligence, particularly chatbots, works and impacts our daily lives—from interacting with technology to connecting with others.

In this unit, students will explore the world of chatbots and how they function by learning about Natural Language Processing (NLP), Large Language Models (LLMs), and machine learning. They will examine how chatbots predict language, improve through feedback, and occasionally make mistakes. The unit will also guide students in investigating how bias can appear in chatbot responses and how the data collected from the internet shapes these outputs. In addition, students will reflect on their moments of human connection, recognize patterns in their social interactions, and consider how technology and AI can enhance or disrupt these experiences. Finally, they will discuss the responsible use of AI in academic settings by analyzing standard AI tools, weighing their benefits and challenges, and working together to establish thoughtful classroom norms for AI use. Through interactive discussions, analysis, and personal reflection, students will build foundational knowledge of AI and develop critical thinking skills about how it should be used in their lives and learning.

**Prerequisite**: [What is AI?](http://dayofai.org/curriculum)

## **Requirements**

* Internet access  
* Projector  
* Whiteboard, blackboard, or chart paper

# **Lesson 1: What are Chatbots and How Do They Work? | Approx. 60 Minutes** {#lesson-1:-what-are-chatbots-and-how-do-they-work?-|-approx.-60-minutes}

### **Objectives**

* Define what a chatbot is and how it works.  
* Understand the basics of NLP, LLMs, and machine learning.  
* Explain how chatbots predict language and learn over time.

###  **Vocabulary**

* **Algorithm**, n. a set of steps or rules to follow to solve a problem or accomplish a specific goal  
* **Chatbot**, n. a computer program that can have conversations with people online  
* **Dataset**, n. an organized group of data  
* **Hallucinations**, AI Outputs that are not true.  
* **Large Language Model**, n. can predict and generate human-like responses by analyzing large amounts of text data  
* **Learning Algorithm:** a set of instructions that helps a computer get better at doing something by practicing with examples.  
* **Machine Learning Models:** computer programs that learn from data instead of being told every single step by a human.  
* **Natural Language Processing** (NLP) is a field of artificial intelligence that helps computers understand, interpret, and respond to human language. It breaks down and analyzes the structure of sentences to make sense of the input.  
* **Neural Network**, n. a computer system designed to copy how the human brain learns. It finds patterns in words, pictures, and numbers to make good guesses.  
* **Pixel,** is a single point in a picture. On the monitor of a computer, a pixel is usually a square. Every pixel has a color and all the pixels together are the picture.  
* **Prediction:** In AI, the process of guessing what comes next in a sentence or interaction based on data.  
* **Probability,** n. the likelihood of something happening or being the case.  
* **Reinforcement Learning**, n. a technique for teaching by providing continuous feedback on successful and unsuccessful behavior. 


### **Resources** {#resources}

[Slide Deck](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/10BBQZIO6kfWwYR2FtGJ7ghm23ldhIAAyPysKLdj6p-0/edit?usp=sharing)  
[Lesson 1 Folder](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1Znfsynr0_3MX1S49GYI65wfE1DLIxo-b?usp=drive_link)  
Article: [Teens are spilling dark thoughts to AI chatbots. Who's to blame when something goes wrong?](https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2025-02-25/teens-are-spilling-dark-thoughts-to-ai-chatbots-whos-to-blame-when-something-goes-wrong)  
Optional Video: [What are LLMs?](https://youtu.be/xD1lOfbMJ0g?feature=shared) 

**Preparation Notes:** If you want to discuss the article used in the warm-up in more depth, it is suggested that you allow students to read it before lesson 1\.

**Activity Steps**

1) Distribute the note-taking worksheets. Explain to students that they will use these worksheets to take notes and respond to questions throughout the lesson. **Warm-up:** Begin the lesson by sharing the headline from the article, [Teens are spilling dark thoughts to AI chatbots. Who's to blame when something goes wrong?](https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2025-02-25/teens-are-spilling-dark-thoughts-to-ai-chatbots-whos-to-blame-when-something-goes-wrong) Ask students to share their use of chatbots and how the article's title makes them feel.  Make sure to discuss what “connection” means. Note the class definition on chart paper if needed.  
2) Continue the lesson by sharing a few places where chatbots can be found and asking students where else they have seen a chatbot appear. Allow students time to respond to their worksheets.  
3) Share the simple definition of a chatbot and ask students to respond to the question  
   1) Can a chatbot make people feel connected?   
   2) Why or why not?

   

4) Then, introduce lesson 1 and share the objectives for the lesson.  
5) Continue to explain how chatbots work, using the slides for discussion and definition sharing. At this point, you can utilize the [video](https://youtu.be/xD1lOfbMJ0g?feature=shared) explaining large language models.   
6) Since this is a complex topic, we have **hidden** the slides explaining Natural Language Processing. If your students understand the material adequately, you can elaborate on It.  
7) After the video, you can break down LLMs using the slides. 

![][image1]  
8\. When explaining this visual model, use these discussion points:

 **Dataset**

“Chatbots start by being trained on huge text collections—like books, websites, conversations, articles, and more. This is called the **dataset**. Think of it as the library the AI learns from.”

 **Learning Algorithm**

“The dataset goes into a computer program called a **learning algorithm**. This is like a recipe that helps the AI practice using all the text examples to learn how language works. It makes many guesses and learns from its mistakes, just like we do when learning something new.”

**Prediction**

“Now comes the fun part—**prediction**. When you type something into a chatbot, it uses what it learned to predict the next word, phrase, or sentence. This prediction becomes the **AI-generated response**.”

9\. Continue to highlight the bottom box. Explain how the AI learns over time:

🧠 **Learn Language**  
 “The AI-first learns how grammar and words work.”

💬 **Learn Conversation**  
 “Then it practices how conversations flow—like questions and answers.”

👍 **Learn Human-Preferred Conversation**  
 “Finally, it gets feedback from humans to improve how helpful or polite its answers are. This helps it improve at giving the responses we prefer.”

10\. Continue and explain to the students that you will break down each step from the illustration. Beginning with datasets.

11\. Students must recognize that the dataset is huge and contains more information than we can imagine. Explain how the dataset is created on the “step by step” slide.

12\. Pose the question: What is a learning algorithm? Share the slide explaining how to shoot a basketball into a basketball hoop. 

13\. Explain the nuances of AI learning language, using the example of humans learning language. Define neural networks for students, then work through each example. 

14\. When you get to “How Words Connect,” explain: The model gets fed all of the text from the billions of language sources. Each time it looks at a new block of text \- a paragraph, a website, an essay, etc. \- it does the following:

1. Pass those word chunks into its neural network  
2. Get the neural network’s prediction for what words, sentences, etc. should come next  
3. Check whether the words it predicts should go next are the same as those in the given paragraph, website, etc.  
4. If they don’t match, update the neural network values to do better next time  
5. Do steps 1-4 billions of times.

15\. **OPTIONAL**: you can also share the animation to explain neural networks further. 

16\. For the last part of the section, you will share the slides that say, “How Do Chatbots Predict Words?”  Read the text “The boy walked his…” and then say:

* “The chatbot doesn’t write the whole sentence at once. Instead, it guesses **one word at a time**—starting with the most likely next word. In this case, it thinks the next word might be **‘dog’** because it’s seen that phrase before in its training data.”  
* “After that, it continues guessing what might come next—maybe **‘to,’** then **‘the,’** and finally **‘park.’** The whole sentence becomes:

  *‘The boy walked his dog to the park.”*  Emphasize the points in the blue box on the slide. 


17\. For the next part, you will show the students how chatbots learn to have conversations through a simple example.  Remind students that “Chatbots try to follow the flow of conversation, but sometimes they make strange or silly mistakes—like responding with ‘pizza’ when it doesn’t fit. That’s because they don’t *understand* what we’re saying like humans do. They’re guessing based on patterns from their training data.”

18\. Continue to share how human feedback influences outputs by sharing the slides that model how actual humans provide feedback by answering questions.  This is a good opportunity to discuss how a human’s bias may affect conversion practice. Say to students, “For example, what if the Duolingo app is unavailable for humans to utilize, and this changes the feedback they provide? How does it change the conversation practice?“

19\. To end the lesson, ask students how this might go wrong and share the example of Google’s AI overview suggesting adding glue to pizza. Ask students   
“Where did the AI overview get its information?” Show students it came from a Reddit post. Ask students to share their responses to this error. This end discussion will set the stage for lesson 2\! 

# **Lesson 2: Exploring Bias in Chatbots/Interrogating the Internet | Approx. 60 Minutes** {#lesson-2:-exploring-bias-in-chatbots/interrogating-the-internet-|-approx.-60-minutes}

# **Objectives**

* # Understand how biases can appear in chatbot responses.

* # Learn about the role of datasets in shaping chatbot outputs.

* # Identify how biases from the internet influence chatbot responses.

#### **Vocabulary**

**Bias, n.** the action of supporting or opposing a particular person or thing or category of people or things in an unfair (and often hidden) way.  
**Dataset**, n. an organized group of data  
**Echo chamber,** n. is when someone mostly hears ideas and opinions they already agree with. This can make their beliefs feel stronger, but it also means they might not get to hear or think about other points of view.  
**Internet, n.** a vast, global network of interconnected computers that allows people to share information and communicate with each other. 

**Resources**

* # [Slide Deck](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/10BBQZIO6kfWwYR2FtGJ7ghm23ldhIAAyPysKLdj6p-0/edit?usp=sharing)

* # [Worksheet for bias analysis](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1DIUDUy8GlzcdXWR5MaCe4I1ZgJqILUwlcIyAPuJWVEc/edit?usp=sharing)

* [Teacher resource guide](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1fZ1B9VwvrSmSydbY4pDCJ-0JHuCNuckFapBnkZLnt7c/edit?usp=sharing)  
* [Real World Examples](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1frqXCMEcLhQXmo8KgIxAgW-_kYQiDMIUL9Z2MKb1VV8/edit?usp=sharing) (teacher guide)  
* Optional Extension: [Source Evaluation Checklist](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HtYEjpc8ciTut_bxAKk1du3aMXZhZfERSzxHuXBNOTg/edit?usp=sharing)

#### **Preparation Notes**

Since this lesson requires students to look through various internet sources, it may be easier to provide them with the [sources](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1frqXCMEcLhQXmo8KgIxAgW-_kYQiDMIUL9Z2MKb1VV8/edit?usp=sharing) to avoid mishaps. There is also an optional activity where you discuss the validity of the AI response students may receive when researching on the internet. This [activity](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HtYEjpc8ciTut_bxAKk1du3aMXZhZfERSzxHuXBNOTg/edit?usp=sharing) can be done at the end of the lesson or before students are working on their group assignments. 

**Activity Steps**

1. # Warm-up. Share the lesson objectives, and then the slide will reintroduce the internet. Share the information about the internet and ask, “Think about this for a moment: How does it make you feel?” Allow students time to share their feelings that the internet is a mix of facts, opinions, and fiction. 

2. # Remind students that they discussed the dataset for chatbots in the previous lesson and reshare the examples. 

3. Begin discussing the meaning of bias using the “pizza glue” example from lesson 1\. Review the definition of bias.  
4. Continue to introduce the “Interrogating the Internet” activity. Explain that interrogating means asking a lot of questions to get information.   
5. Categorizing the Internet: for this slide, ask students to think about how we categorize the information we see across the Internet. This may seem arduous, but if students struggle, share the categories on the following slide.    
6. After you have gone through the categories, begin the activity by modeling it with students. Share information on “**News Articles and Media Reports”** and examples. Pose these questions:  
   1. What is the difference between a riot and a demonstration?  
   2. Impact on a chatbot?   
   3. What is the intent?  
   4. What assumptions are being made?  
   5. Who might benefit or be harmed by this information?  
7. Discuss the students’ answers and agree on how this information could influence a chatbot and peoples’ perceptions.  
8. Continue with the examples from around the Internet. Using the provided questions, guide students through analyzing how data sources influence responses.  
9. After the provided examples on the slides, assign students to work on further internet interrogations on the [Exploring Bias on the Internet worksheets](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1DIUDUy8GlzcdXWR5MaCe4I1ZgJqILUwlcIyAPuJWVEc/edit?usp=sharing). This can be done individually, in pairs, or in small groups.

   Since this work requires students to **look for bias on the internet in various categories,** you can edit the worksheet and/or complete all the examples as a class activity in a controlled environment.  Alternatively, you can find examples of each and provide them to students to analyze with the worksheet.  We have compiled examples [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1frqXCMEcLhQXmo8KgIxAgW-_kYQiDMIUL9Z2MKb1VV8/edit?usp=sharing). 

10. Utilize the [Internet Interrogation Teacher Resource](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1fZ1B9VwvrSmSydbY4pDCJ-0JHuCNuckFapBnkZLnt7c/edit?usp=sharing) as needed.   
11. After completing all the examples, use an additional class period for students to share their findings. This will depend on how you choose to assign the remainder of the examples.  
12. Students must have time to reflect on their findings at the end of this lesson.  In addition to the questions on their worksheets and the slides, you may also want them to discuss:   
    1. how bias in chatbots could impact real-world interactions.  
    2. How can we minimize bias in AI systems?

**Optional Extension:**  Before allowing students to work on their Exploring Bias on the Internet assignment, discuss how it has become easy to accept our first response in an Internet search. Share these [guidelines](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HtYEjpc8ciTut_bxAKk1du3aMXZhZfERSzxHuXBNOTg/edit?usp=sharing) with students and demonstrate how they should be wary of the first answer they receive. Use the article provided and the answer key as needed.

# [**Lesson 3: Mapping Our Moments of Connection and How AI Shapes Them| Approx. 60 Minutes**](#lesson-3:-mapping-our-moments-of-connection-and-how-ai-shapes-them|-approx.-60-minutes) {#lesson-3:-mapping-our-moments-of-connection-and-how-ai-shapes-them|-approx.-60-minutes}

# 

# **Objectives**

* Students will identify and reflect on moments of human connection throughout their day.  
* Students will recognize patterns in their social interactions and assess how they feel during these moments.  
* Students will analyze how AI influences human connection, both positively and negatively.  
* Students will identify personal habits that impact their social interactions.

#### **Vocabulary**

**Connection n.** a relationship in which a person, thing, or idea is linked or associated with something else.

**Resources**  
[Slide Deck](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/10BBQZIO6kfWwYR2FtGJ7ghm23ldhIAAyPysKLdj6p-0/edit?usp=sharing)  
[Lesson 3 Worksheet](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1j-sHo9T5QegRT-Vbkp5wrEmr4byNYBMv3Dtj_9ZX4vQ/edit?usp=sharing)

**Optional Lesson/Extension:** [Exploring the Impact of AI Chatbots on Human Connection](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1RkJUwot5O3IJa9p3iRjjWeF1E65_ZaD1JlwM_hwQliI/edit?usp=sharing)

**Preparation Notes:** To save time during classwork, introduce the Daily Connection Chart and assign it for homework before the lesson. 

#### **Activity Steps**

1. Warm up and begin the lesson by asking, "What does connection mean to you?" Encourage students to describe different connection forms (e.g., verbal, physical, emotional, digital). If needed, pose these follow-up questions,  
* When do you feel most connected to others?  
* When do you feel disconnected?  
* How does technology (phones, social media, video games, AI assistants) affect your connections?

#### 

2. Continue with the lesson by introducing the “Daily Connection Chart.” Use the example provided to show students how t[hey will complete the chart](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1j-sHo9T5QegRT-Vbkp5wrEmr4byNYBMv3Dtj_9ZX4vQ/edit?usp=sharing). Students will create a timeline of their previous day, marking key moments of human connection. It may also be helpful to introduce this worksheet before the lesson so that students complete the chart for homework.   
   * Label who they interacted with (family, friends, teachers, strangers, online vs. in-person).  
   * Describe how they interacted (face-to-face conversation, texting, gaming, social media, calling, AI interaction).  
   * Reflect on how it made them feel (e.g., happy, distracted, distant, supported).

##### **Sample Answers**

| Time | Who? | How? | Feeling |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 7:30 AM | Family | Talking over breakfast | Connected, happy |
| 10:00 AM | Classmate | Whispering in class | Engaged, distracted |
| 4:00 PM | Friend | Texting | Close, but distant |
| 8:00 PM | Alexa (AI) | Asking about homework | Neutral |

3. #### Once students have completed their charts, have them analyze and share their responses, using these questions as a guide. Students should write their reflections on the same worksheet.  You may also have students swap with a partner so the partner can analyze their chart.  As a class, ask several students to share their responses: 

* What patterns do you notice in your connections?  
* Were any moments surprisingly meaningful?  
* Did you notice times when you could have connected more deeply?  
4. This assignment's next “layer” asks students to look at their charts again from a technology and media perspective.   
5. Students look back at their daily connection charts and then answer the following:   
   1. Where were most of your connections happening?  
   2. How did digital vs. face-to-face interactions feel different?  
   3. Did technology make some connections stronger? Weaker?  
6. Students can also share their answers with a partner at this time.

7. #### **AI Influence Brainstorm:** collaboratively list ways AI is part of our social interactions. Students should be able to assist in generating ideas, but here are some to ensure you include. This list can live on a chart paper or slide deck. Students can copy down their answers on the [worksheet](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1j-sHo9T5QegRT-Vbkp5wrEmr4byNYBMv3Dtj_9ZX4vQ/edit?usp=sharing) provided or create their own personalized list. 

   * Social media recommendations (TikTok, Instagram)  
   * Autocorrect and predictive text  
   * Chatbots and virtual assistants (Siri, Alexa)  
   * Video game matchmaking  
   * AI-generated content (Snapchat AI, YouTube suggestions)  
   * Online messaging algorithms (read receipts, typing indicators)

   

8. Transition to the next part of this activity by saying, *“Now that we’ve brainstormed how AI shows up in our social interactions, let's take a closer look at its impact. Not all influences are positive or negative—they can strengthen or erode connections. To dig deeper, we will create a T-Chart to sort these AI-driven interactions into two categories: those that help us feel more connected and those that might actually pull us apart.”* You can change the headings as needed or explain that **erode** is another way of saying “pull us apart.” Students should complete this activity on their own [worksheets](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1j-sHo9T5QegRT-Vbkp5wrEmr4byNYBMv3Dtj_9ZX4vQ/edit?usp=sharing) as well.   
9. Continue to say,” *Think back to our shared ideas and consider how each affects our relationships. Does it bring people closer or create distance? You can use the examples from our brainstorm or add new ones. Let’s start organizing our thoughts.*” 

**SAMPLE ANSWERS**

| Strengthens Connection | Erodes Connection |
| :---- | :---- |
| Video calls with family | Endless scrolling on social media |
| AI chatbots helping with mental health | AI-generated content keeping us glued to screens |
| Gaming with friends online | Texting instead of face-to-face conversations |

10. #### After creating the list, there are two options. 1\.  Split the class into two groups—one arguing that AI strengthens human connection and the other arguing it weakens it. Each side presents at least three points before discussing them as a whole class. Or 2\. Ask students:  What is one habit you might change after today’s discussion?" Utilize the [worksheets](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1j-sHo9T5QegRT-Vbkp5wrEmr4byNYBMv3Dtj_9ZX4vQ/edit?usp=sharing) as needed for this assignment.

11. Students should walk away from the lesson's discussions with newfound understanding and connections in their everyday lives and how AI shapes them. 

**Optional Lesson/Extension:** [Exploring the Impact of AI Chatbots on Human Connection](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1RkJUwot5O3IJa9p3iRjjWeF1E65_ZaD1JlwM_hwQliI/edit?usp=sharing)

	This lesson can replace lesson 3 or be an additional lesson for students to build on their understanding of AI Chatbots and Human Connections. 

**Lesson 4: Creating Our Classroom AI Usage Norms| Approx. 60 minutes**

# **Objectives**

* Discuss the potential benefits and drawbacks of using AI in schoolwork.  
* Collaboratively create a set of classroom norms for responsibly using AI tools.  
* Examine various AI tools and use cases, discussing the benefits, challenges, and impacts on learning and personal accomplishment.  
* Come to a consensus on when it may be appropriate to use AI for a school assignment

#### **Resources**

[Slide Deck](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/10BBQZIO6kfWwYR2FtGJ7ghm23ldhIAAyPysKLdj6p-0/edit?usp=sharing)  
[AI Usage Self-Reflection](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1aNRJ1qhIKAl-41AJ1VW-dnhDgbu7zLqAK1YB-Ff59G8/edit?usp=sharing)  
[AI Use/Who’s Doing the Thinking? Student Worksheet](https://docs.google.com/document/d/17TQ9cCBGZsdAxneFLHbXlMuClI0f83sSVKpEmEpWrxo/edit?usp=sharing)  
[AI Assignment Teacher Guide](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1sheSPTPFzC9uBo7DO-8YyiqIBUORmAUZX9ofGrwpmt4/edit?usp=sharing)

**Preparation Notes:**   
You should assign self-reflection before class to save time during the lesson.  
This activity can be tailored to the subject(s) you teach. Please review the student worksheets and customize the assignments to meet your student's needs. 

#### **Activity Steps**

1. Warm-up:  Ask students if they have ever used AI tools (e.g., grammar checkers, calculators, voice assistants). Have students share the results of their AI Usage self-assessment. As students share, document any themes or patterns that arise across their responses on a slide or piece of chart paper. Students should answer the question: **What similarities and differences do you notice?** on their worksheet.

2. ### The warm-up activity and discussion will be used to transition to the next section: “Using AI: Who is Doing the Thinking?”

3. For this part of the activity, you will model the activity that students will complete with groups or partnerships. Pose the scenario: “your social studies teacher asked you to research a historical figure and write an essay about them.”  
4. As a class, brainstorm the steps needed to complete the essay. Use the first step provided on the chart to model to students how they will complete this activity with their groups. Continue writing out each step for writing an essay and completing the chart. 

**SAMPLE ANSWERS**

## **Write a Five-Paragraph Essay**

| Step | Can AI Help? | Should AI Help? | Benefits | Challenges |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Brainstorm a topic | Yes | Maybe | Helps generate ideas | Might discourage original thinking |
| Research information | Yes | Yes | Finds sources quickly | May miss reliable or age-appropriate sources |
| Create an outline | Yes | Maybe | Can suggest structure | Might limit creativity or unique ideas |
| Write a draft | Yes | Maybe | Produces quick content | Can reduce student writing practice |
| Edit for grammar and clarity | Yes | Yes | Improves grammar and tone | May over-correct voice or tone |

## 

5. ### After thoroughly modeling the activity, distribute the [worksheet](https://docs.google.com/document/d/17TQ9cCBGZsdAxneFLHbXlMuClI0f83sSVKpEmEpWrxo/edit?usp=sharing) for students to complete independently. You may pre-assign the assignments for students to analyze or use the options provided [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1sheSPTPFzC9uBo7DO-8YyiqIBUORmAUZX9ofGrwpmt4/edit?usp=sharing). 

6. As students are completing the assignment, make sure they are taking time to reflect on the questions provided among each other:   
   1. Where was AI support most helpful?  
   2. Where did it seem to undermine the learning process?  
   3. Were there any disagreements within your group?  
7. After ample time, bring the class together for a whole-group discussion to share their findings, opinions, and responses. You can also document responses on a slide or chart paper.   
8. Once you have given students time to share their experiences, you will direct them to the final part of the group discussion, which will require them to draft guidelines for AI usage.  
9. Each group drafts a set of 4–6 **“AI Use Guidelines”** for the specific assignment they analyzed (e.g., writing an essay solving a math problem). If needed, provide the sentence starters and example templates for students. Alternatively, you can assign this for homework.   
10. **Optional**: Provide a template for students to justify their AI Use guidelines:

    

| Guideline | Why? (Justification) |
| :---- | :---- |
| Example: Use AI to check grammar after writing a first draft. | It helps polish writing without taking over the thinking process. |

    

11. Gallery Walk: After students have had time to draft their use guidelines, allow them to read each other’s and provide feedback. Students can add their guidelines to chart paper or a slide deck. If using chart paper, provide students with post-it notes to comment on each other’s work. Create a system where students can show their support for a guideline.  
12. Have each group share one "most important" and one "most debated" guideline. As they share, track overlapping ideas and note differences across assignments.  
13. Work together to create a **classwide set of AI norms** that:  
* Are assignment-specific (e.g., one for essays, one for projects)  
* Clarify expectations for independent thinking  
* Encourage responsible and transparent AI use. 

14. **Consensus Building:** Vote or agree on the most important norms to follow.  Post these in your classroom or share them digitally as a living document\!

15.  It is important to note that these norms may change over time and need to be edited/updated.
